summary:
NASA has been watching fires from space with MODIS since 2000, but MODIS is close to retirement. Its replacement, VIIRS, has sharper eyes and picks up about twice as many fires. So if you just glue the two records together, you get nonsense. We tried it on six places in Kazakhstan and Argentina, and in three of them the trend came out backwards. In Corrientes, Argentina, the glued data says fires went up 81%. They actually went down 19%.
We built Wildfire Calendar to fix that. For every area and every month, it works out how much more VIIRS sees than MODIS and rescales the old years, so the whole 25-year record sits on one scale. We checked it by hiding a year and predicting it from MODIS alone: the error dropped from about 50% to 11–35%.
The result is a website where you draw any area and see when it usually burns, whether this month is normal, and how any fire compares to every year since 2000. You can download the data as CSV.
details:
We picked this challenge because the problem is simple to state and easy to get wrong. MODIS gives us the longest fire history we have, and it's about to stop. VIIRS carries on, but it sees roughly twice as much fire, and the ratio changes with the season and the landscape. One fixed multiplier doesn't cut it.

How it works

We download the yearly MODIS and VIIRS archives from NASA FIRMS for a country and keep only confident vegetation fires. Instead of counting raw detections we count how many 0.1° cells had fire each day, because that depends less on pixel size. Then, for the area the user picks, we look at the years when both sensors were flying (2013–2025) and work out a VIIRS-to-MODIS factor for each month. The old MODIS-only years get multiplied by that factor. We also handle the early years when only Terra was up, and days when VIIRS was down but MODIS still saw fire.

How we know it works

For every year from 2013 to 2025 we hid that year, learned the factor from the rest, and predicted the hidden year from MODIS alone. With our method the error is 11–35%. Without it, it's 43–59%. The app turns that error into a simple label (High, Medium, Low, or Insufficient when there's too little fire to test), so people know how much to trust the old-vs-new comparison for their area.

We also checked six big fires that made the news: Corrientes 2022, the Paraná Delta 2020, Córdoba 2020, Chubut 2021, Kostanay 2015 and Arakaragai 2022. Every one of them is the biggest week on record for its dates in its area.

What we found

In three of six areas, gluing the sensors together makes fire look like it's increasing when it's actually decreasing. MODIS on its own, flying the whole 25 years, agrees with our corrected numbers, not the glued ones. In the Kostanay steppe in Kazakhstan, fire is down about two thirds since the 2000s, and you see that on Terra, Aqua and VIIRS separately.

What you can do in the app

Draw an area on the map, type coordinates with a radius, or pick an example. You get a month-by-year fire calendar, the main fire seasons, how this month compares to the median, the last 7 days of fires, and a tab where you pick any date range and see where it ranks among all years. Everything can be downloaded as CSV, and every chart can be saved as a picture. The interface works in English, Spanish and Russian.

Who it's for

Fire and forest services planning for the busy season, nature reserves keeping an eye on their land, and researchers who need one consistent record with an honest error attached.

What's not done yet

Weather comes from one point in the middle of the area. The trends tell you that fire changed, not why. Next we want to add the current year through the FIRMS API, bring in the newer NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 satellites, and send a heads-up when a week runs above normal.

Built with Python, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Plotly and Folium. Code: https://github.com/romiisromie/wildfire-calendar
